rationale: The book's core claim — that scripture's pearl-figure denotes the one complete light, the full moon as governor of the appointed times and the gate of entry (the merchant buying his entry at the King's gate) — is carried by a genuinely dense cross-textual web that the common interpretation leaves unexplained: keseh really is 'full moon' in Ps 81:3 and Prov 7:20 (so most modern versions), keseh in Prov 7:20 is spelled letter-for-letter as kisse' 'throne,' Job 26:9 is read 'full moon' by the ESV and others exactly as the book argues, Ps 104:19 assigns the moon to the moedim, and Rev 21:21's insistence that every several gate is ONE pearl — a detail the 'splendor' reading merely labels — is given a functional rationale (gates = appointed times of meeting). The strongest counter (pearl = the kingdom/salvation of supreme worth) is the parable's natural frame and explains the value dimension more simply, but it cannot point to any supplied text that the book's core contradicts; it simply declines to engage the keseh/moed texts and the one-pearl-per-gate peculiarity, and the value dimension is not denied but specified by the book's reading (Isa 33:6 welds treasure and times). Under the governing standard — a counter must explain at least one supplied detail the book's core cannot explain without contradiction — no such detail exists; the counter's advantages amount to simplicity and underdetermination. However, several load-bearing elaborations (the claim that new moon and full moon are one day, the Ezekiel 46 east-gate argument that depends on it, and the repointed Prov 31 portrait) are disputed or fringe, so only the core identification is accepted.
book_core_identification: The pearl symbolizes the one complete, round, white light — the full moon (keseh, the 'fulness' hidden under the KJV's 'throne' and 'time appointed') — as governor of the appointed times (moedim) and as the gate of entry into the kingdom: the one pearl of great price is the appointed time of meeting at the King's gate, and wisdom/the bride priced above pearls (peninim) belong to the same figure.
book_secondary_elaborations: The calendar claim that Ps 81:3 names one day, not two — that the full moon is the head of the month (new moon = keseh)
The Ezekiel 46:1 east-gate argument (gate opened on the new-moon day, entered by the full moon at sunset), which depends on the calendar claim

The full rereading of Proverbs 31:10-31 as a portrait of the moon-bride (palms/kaph as the curved light-receiving vessel, 'clothed in double,' 'laugheth at the last day' as shachaq, halal as 'to shine')
The Daniel 7 throne-room read as full moons set in their stations with the 'Foremost of Days' seated where the month begins
The pairing with a prior 'counterfeit moon covered in darkness' chapter (eclipse imagery, thief climbing in the other way)
Matt 7:6 read as the holy appointed times trampled by the nations (tied to Luke 21:24, Dan 8:13, Rev 11:2)
The bride = moon equation resting on an unsupplied 'Sun, Moon, and Stars' chapter
strongest_counter_interpretation: The pearl symbolizes the kingdom of heaven (or salvation/Christ) as a treasure of supreme, surpassing worth: Matt 13:45-46 pairs with the hidden-treasure parable to teach that the kingdom is worth surrendering everything to obtain; Matt 7:6's pearls are sacred, precious truth not to be profaned; Rev 21:21's pearl gates express the immeasurable glory of the redeemed order; Prov 3:15 and 31:10 are simple hyperbolic comparisons with costly jewels, and the keseh/moon verses (Ps 81:3; Prov 7:20; Job 26:9; Ps 104:19) are about the moon and calendar, not pearls at all.
counter_core_identification: The pearl is the kingdom of heaven itself (or the salvation/Christ found in it) as the object of supreme value, with pearls generally standing for sacred preciousness; it is not a celestial body or a calendar sign.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that the pearl denotes the full moon or the appointed times: scripture nowhere calls the moon a pearl, and the connection between the pearl texts (Matt 13:45-46; 7:6; Rev 21:21; Prov 3:15; 31:10) and the keseh/moed texts (Ps 81:3; Prov 7:20; Job 26:9; Ps 104:19) exists only through the book's unstated extrabiblical premise that the full moon is the sky's pearl; the pearl is the kingdom itself, not a gate or a lunar timekeeper.
counter_case: The parable's own frame is explicit: 'the kingdom of heaven is likened unto a merchant man' — its twin, the hidden treasure (Matt 13:44), teaches the same lesson of supreme value with no celestial referent, so pairing favors the value reading
No verse in either Testament calls the moon a pearl; the identification rests on visual properties (one, round, white) imported from outside the text
peninim is rendered 'rubies' by the KJV and 'corals' by much modern scholarship; Strong's 'probably a pearl' is a conjecture, not an established gloss

Ps 81:3 in virtually all translations distinguishes the new moon (chodesh) from the full moon (keseh) as two feast occasions; the book's one-day reading (month begins at full moon) is a fringe calendar position contradicted by standard Hebrew lexicography
Prov 3:15 and 31:10 say wisdom and the bride are priced ABOVE pearls, which reads most simply as hyperbole over jewels, not as an identification of the bride with a pearl
Rev 21:21 sits amid gold streets and jeweled foundations — a catalogue of splendor, adequately read as the surpassing glory of the city without a calendrical decoding
book_explanatory_advantages: Explains Rev 21:21's odd insistence that every several gate is ONE pearl — twelve gates, one whole pearl each — where the splendor reading treats the detail as decoration

Explains the parable's structure: many goodly pearls but exactly ONE bought at the price of everything ('one' as complete, whole), paralleling Prov 31:29 and Song 6:8-9's one above the many daughters and queens

Recovers a real lexical fact: keseh means 'full moon' (Ps 81:3; Prov 7:20 per NKJV, ESV, NASB, JPS), is spelled כסא in Prov 7:20 identically with kisse' 'throne,' and Job 26:9 is rendered 'full moon' by the ESV and other modern versions — exactly the dual reading the book argues

Ties the pearl texts to an attested lunar office: 'He appointed the moon for seasons/moedim' (Ps 104:19; Gen 1:14), giving the pearl-gates a function (appointed times of meeting) rather than a mere aesthetic

The Hebrew merchandise web is real: 'her merchandise is good' (Prov 31:18) quotes Prov 3:14 letter for letter, and Matt 13:45's merchant seeking goodly pearls completes a three-text thread joining wisdom, the bride, and the pearl

Reads Matt 7:6's trampling with scripture's own trampling idiom — the holy city and sanctuary trodden by the nations 'until the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled' (Luke 21:24; Rev 11:2; Dan 8:13) — connecting pearls and times

Isa 33:6 ('wisdom and knowledge shall be the stability of thy times... the fear of the LORD is his treasure') genuinely joins the treasure and the times in one sentence, answering the paired-parable objection
counter_explanatory_advantages: Requires no extrabiblical premise: value is the parable's explicit and self-contained point, confirmed by the parallel treasure parable
Handles Prov 3:15/31:10 with maximal simplicity as jewel-hyperbole
Preserves the standard two-occasion reading of Ps 81:3 and the standard lexicography distinguishing chodesh from keseh
Does not depend on a disputed rendering of peninim or on repointing the consonantal text of Proverbs 31
decisive_sources: Revelation 21:21 — every several gate of one pearl; the one-pearl-per-gate detail that only the book's reading rationalizes
Psalm 81:3 with Proverbs 7:20 — keseh as 'full moon' in most versions, spelled כסא in Prov 7:20, identical with 'throne'
Job 26:9 — 'the face of his throne/full moon' covered with cloud, the dual reading adopted by the ESV and other modern versions
Psalm 104:19 — the moon appointed for the moedim, supplying the pearl-gate's function
Proverbs 3:14-15 and 31:10, 18 — the peninim/good-merchandise web joining wisdom, the bride, and the merchant of Matt 13:45
Matthew 13:45-46 — the one pearl above the goodly pearls, matching the one-above-the-many structure of Prov 31:29
unresolved_objections: Scripture never explicitly names the moon a pearl; the core identification's final link (one, round, white, at a gate → full moon) is a property-inference, not a stated equation

The claim that new moon and keseh are one day — that the month begins at the full moon — contradicts standard lexicography and nearly all translations of Ps 81:3, and the Ezekiel 46:1 east-gate argument collapses without it
peninim as 'pearl' rests on Strong's 'probably'; much scholarship reads corals or rubies
The bride = moon equation is imported from an unsupplied prior chapter ('Sun, Moon, and Stars') rather than established from the printed evidence
The Proverbs 31 rereading depends on repointings and minority elder-version choices (e.g., 'clothed in double,' 'laugheth at the last day') that are contestable word by word

The paired hidden-treasure parable remains most naturally read as the supreme value of the kingdom itself, so the value dimension of the common reading survives inside the book's reading rather than being displaced
